Which basically says a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. Filtering the data doesn't stop it.

Here they claim RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at small k (e.g., k = 1), but the base models achieve a higher pass@k score when k is large. -----

This is neat because you have a nice system design lever, but you gotta be cautious because one says distillation can add capabilities the base model lacked. The other says distillation also passes along traits you never meant to copy in the first place. 

RL to sharpen, distillation to learn? But then you might sharpen the wrong thing. Tricky stuff.

article.plain_text:
Eight ways multi-step agents go wrong, the structural answers teams have tried, and what each one measurably buys and costs
Quick grasp
What. An agent architecture is a set of model calls plus the rules that decide what each call sees, what it may do, and what it returns. The useful unit is not "an agent" but a node: one role with one context policy, one tool list, one budget, and one output format. A planner, a worker that gets one brief, a reviewer that sees the diff but not the author's reasoning, a guard that reads a document and cannot act, a curator that writes memory while nobody waits. Architecture is the choice of nodes and of what crosses between them.
Why it matters. Most agent failures are structural, not a weak model. 
A wrong early step steers later steps. 
A hand-off in prose drops the facts the receiver needed. 
A catalogue of fifty tools makes the model pick the wrong one. 
Five copies of the same model agree on the same mistake. 
A reviewer that shares the author's context approves the author's work. 
Each of these has a structural fix, and each fix has a measured cost. The job is to match the fix to the failure you actually have, because a fix applied to the wrong failure is pure overhead.
How, in five steps.
Name the failure you see in traces, using the eight cases below: a step that poisons later steps, a lossy hand-off, too much in view, correlated mistakes, an input bigger than the window, a dependent reviewer, latency or cost, or no learning across sessions.
Find the boundary where the failure crosses: between attempts, between nodes, between the catalogue and the call, between author and reviewer, between sessions.
Pick the structural answer for that boundary from the level that matches, and read its measured cost before its measured gain.
Define what crosses the boundary as a schema with required fields, a "need more" return, and a budget, then test the payload like an API.
Measure the gain on tasks you control against a single agent with the same token budget, because most published gains shrink or reverse once the budget is equalised.
When to care. Two conditions: the job takes more than one model call, and at least one call can go wrong. If every task is a single clean call, structure only adds cost. If calls chain, retry, branch, or run for hours, the wiring between them decides whether failures stay local or compound.
Important: The strongest controlled results in this area are negative. At equal token budgets a single agent usually matches or beats a team, and five copies of one model make the same mistake five times. Every pattern below earns its place only by adding something a single call cannot have: a clean context, a different model, a signal the author did not write, or a read the window cannot hold.
The level tree
Level 1: One failed step steers every later step: fresh context per attempt, restart loops, checkpoints, and durable retries.
Level 2: The hand-off drops what the receiver needed: typed state, file-backed task packets, structured relays, gists, and rebuild-by-inputs plans.
Level 3: Too much in view: progressive disclosure, routers, per-node catalogues, and the cost of nesting.
Level 4: More agents, same mistakes: correlated failure, conformity, error amplification, and the structures that keep workers independent.
Level 5: The input is bigger than any window: orchestrator-workers, chunk and reduce, recursive reads, code execution, and cheap readers.
Level 6: The reviewer agrees with the author and the reader trusts the document: blind verifiers, cross-model review, hidden graders, guard nodes, and failure attribution.
Level 7: The clock and the bill: fast and slow nodes, planner-executor splits, routing by cost, caching, and budgets per node.
Level 8: Nothing learned across sessions: memory curators, sleep-time compute, and why plain history still wins.
Level 1: One failed step steers every later step
This level answers: when an early call fails or guesses wrong, what stops that failure from biasing everything the system does next?
This is the most common structural failure and the one with the clearest evidence. A model that sees its own wrong turn in context treats it as part of the story and keeps going in the same direction.
Laban and colleagues (arXiv 2505.06120), 15 models, 200,000 or more simulated conversations: splitting a task's instructions across turns cut accuracy by 39% on average; aptitude fell 16% but unreliability rose 112%.
A recap pasted into the same conversation recovered only about 15 to 20% of the loss; a fresh conversation seeded with a consolidated statement recovered most of it.
Self-conditioning (arXiv 2509.09677): seeing its own earlier mistakes raised a model's later error rate; the authors attribute about 20% of GAIA failures, 48% of ALFWorld failures and 33% of WebShop failures to this, and find extended thinking reduces it.
Memory Curse (arXiv 2605.08060): agents carrying full history in a repeated cooperation game cooperated 92.1% of the time early and 20.6% late; the history itself drove the collapse.
Chroma's context rot study (vendor measurement, 18 models): a focused prompt of about 300 tokens beat the full transcript of about 113,000 tokens on LongMemEval, and shuffled transcripts scored higher than coherent ones.
The unreliability number is the one that matters. The models did not get much weaker; they became erratic because a wrong assumption stayed in the input. The Chroma result says the same thing from the other side: coherent history hurt more than shuffled history, so the model was following the narrative of its own context, not just failing to find facts in it. Breunig's name for this is context poisoning, and it is distinct from the older position effects, where accuracy depends on where a fact sits in a long window (arXiv 2307.03172; NoLiMa, arXiv 2502.05167, where 11 of 13 models fell below half their short-context score at 32,000 tokens).
Six structural answers exist, and they differ mainly in where the cut falls.
A fresh context per attempt. The task runs in a node that starts empty, with a written brief and nothing else, and is discarded afterwards. The chatbot version is a stateful front node that holds the conversation and writes the brief for a stateless worker; the worker's failures never enter the chat. Framework defaults vary: OpenAI Agents SDK "agents as tools", Google ADK AgentTool and Strands .as_tool() start the callee empty, while hand-offs and sub_agents pass the transcript.
The restart loop. Run the agent on a fixed prompt file, exit, run again in a new context, repeat until tests pass or a budget is spent; files and test results are the only state. Advocates report about 259 pull requests in 30 days from one loop and an effective window of roughly 147,000 to 152,000 tokens before quality fell. Both figures are anecdotes with no control.
Checkpoint and rewind. Go back to before the wrong turn rather than correcting after it. Claude Code's guidance says to clear and restart after two failed corrections, and its checkpoints can restore the code, the conversation, or both; Cursor's checkpoints restore files only and leave the messages in place, so the wrong turn stays in context.
Durable retry per step. Runtimes such as Temporal, Restate, Inngest and DBOS record each step and replay from the last completed one; a model call wrapped as a step gets a fresh attempt with its original inputs. Temporal retries without limit by default, DBOS three times. The trap is that a tool returning an error as a string counts as a success, so the error is recorded as a result and replayed into every resume.
Keep errors inside the attempt. Manus's production rule is the opposite of all of the above on its face: keep the failed action and its error in context, because a model that sees its failure adjusts and one that does not repeats it.
Thinking before acting. The self-conditioning study found extended thinking reduced the effect, which is the cheapest answer when a reset is not possible.
The Manus rule and the Laban result are not in conflict once the time scale is fixed. Within one attempt, the failed command and its error are evidence the model needs. Across attempts, once the task restarts, the old failure is no longer evidence, it is bias. The rule that fits both: keep errors inside an attempt, drop them across attempts, and when something must cross, write the lesson and not the trace.
The second trap is subtler. If the front node pastes every worker failure back into the conversation verbatim, it accumulates exactly the traces the split was meant to isolate. Isolation works only if both directions of the boundary are filtered: the worker gets a brief, and the front node gets a conclusion.
What it means for us: Decide the time scale before picking the cut. Inside one attempt the error is evidence; across attempts it is bias. Fresh contexts, restart loops and durable retries all implement the second half, and all of them fail silently if an error is returned as text instead of raised as a failure.
Carry forward
A fresh context removes the wrong turn; a recap in the same context recovers a fraction of the loss.
Keep errors inside one attempt and drop them across attempts; cross the boundary with a lesson and a file path.
Any retry mechanism that records an error string as a result replays the poison.
Level 2: The hand-off drops what the receiver needed
This level answers: when work crosses from one node to another, what is lost, and which payload formats lose the least?
Every cut that fixes Level 1 creates this problem. The receiving node cannot know what it was not told, and the sender does not know what the receiver will need.
Natural-Language Agent Harnesses (arXiv 2603.25723): "information hand-off recall", the share of facts a parent needed that a child's reply contained, was 0.32 on software tasks and 0.55 on terminal tasks, against 1.00 for a single agent that did the work itself.
The Specification Gap (arXiv 2603.24284, n = 204): a single agent with the full specification scored 88.6%; a parallel team where each worker saw a slice scored 58.2%; giving the merger the full specification restored 88.9%, while asking workers to report conflicts added nothing.
Relay chains (arXiv 2603.26993v1, n = 200 MMLU questions): a single agent scored 90.7%; passing conclusions in prose through two, three and five agents gave 41.2%, 43.5% and 22.5%; a structured relay that passed a probability over answers instead of prose kept 75.2%.
📷
The relay result is the sharpest. Five agents in prose scored below random guessing on a four-option test, and the same chain with a structured payload lost a fifth of the single-agent score instead of three quarters. The payload format, not the number of agents, decided most of the loss. The paper's theory section adds the general point: a central decision maker with the same signals is never worse than a delegated network, so any gain from splitting must come from something the split adds. Cognition's essay names the mechanism as "actions carry implicit decisions": a worker that sees only a brief cannot know which options were already rejected upstream.
Eight structural answers appear in the record, ordered from cheapest to most invasive.
Typed state instead of transcript. Nodes exchange a defined set of fields, each with a rule for how updates merge, and a sub-graph exposes only its answer. LangGraph's graph state and POLARIS's type-checked plan graphs (arXiv 2601.11816) are the reference designs. The cost is that a fact with no field is lost, so a free-text notes field is needed for the unexpected.
File-backed task packets. The NLAH paper's own fix is a task file, a response file, and an append-only history on disk, so the receiver can read more than the sender summarised. Adding file-backed state alone lifted the software score from 73.0 to 75.6 and the computer-use score from 44.4 to 58.3.
The merger sees everything. The specification-gap result says where to spend context: give the node that combines results the full specification, not the workers.
Structured relay. Pass a distribution or a scored list rather than a conclusion, as the relay study did; the receiver sees the sender's uncertainty, not only its pick.
Compact verified gists. DELM (arXiv 2606.10662) has peers write verified 100-token gists to shared state and unfold detail only on demand; the same task cost $0.125 against $0.399 when peers read full command histories.
Restorable compression. Manus's rule: keep the file path or URL and drop the content, so the receiver can re-read what the summary left out. Compression that cannot be undone is a hand-off with no return channel.
Rebuild by inputs, not by age. Planfence (arXiv 2609.03340) tested plans that go stale when a peer's memory changes: age-checked plans let outdated plans through in 30 of 30 five-agent workflows; plans rebuilt whenever their inputs changed let 0 through, at about 15% more tokens.
Latent hand-off. Recursive Multi-Agent Systems (arXiv 2604.25917) pass hidden states instead of text through trained link modules: an average gain of 8.3% over text baselines across 9 benchmarks with 34.6 to 75.6% fewer tokens. It needs model access that closed APIs do not give, so it is a research result for now.
Two more results belong here because they are about what crosses, not where. The Hallucination Snowball study (arXiv 2608.14588) modelled a four-stage pipeline and measured how many errors survived to the end.
Errors surviving the pipeline: 58.4% with no checks and 16.2% with a gate at every boundary.
A gate at each hand-off is the structural version of "validate at the boundary". The second result is from reading framework source rather than papers. The OpenAI Agents SDK filter remove_all_tools strips tool-call items from a hand-off history, but a tool result quoted inside an assistant message survives, so a failed lookup can cross as prose. A filter written to drop failed tool results has to be written for that case.
The last answer is a return channel. A worker that cannot ask back is the main cost of every split, so the brief needs a "need more information" return value that the sender turns into a question, and a schema with required fields so a missing input fails before the worker runs rather than inside it.
Why it matters: The format of the payload decided most of the loss in every study that varied it. A prose summary kept a quarter of the single-agent score; a structured one kept three quarters; a file the receiver could re-read added two to fourteen points. Design the hand-off before the nodes.
Carry forward
What crosses the boundary decides most of the loss; structured beats prose, and a re-readable file beats both.
The node that merges results needs the full specification; the workers do not.
Gate every hand-off, write filters for the leak you mean to stop, and give every worker a way to say "need more".
Level 3: Too much in view
This level answers: how much of the tool and skill catalogue should any node see at once, and what does it cost to show more?
Breunig's second and third failure names are context distraction, where so much history is present that the model repeats past actions, and context confusion, where irrelevant tools or instructions get used because they are there. Both come from showing a node more than its role needs.
The evidence that confusion is real comes from counting tools.
RAG-MCP (arXiv 2505.03275): retrieving relevant tool descriptions before the call raised selection accuracy from 13.62% to 43.13% and roughly halved prompt tokens.
Production telemetry on MCP servers (arXiv 2606.30317, about 200 turns per bucket, not controlled): Haiku 4.5 picked the right tool 91% of the time with 10 tools and 87% with 15; Sonnet 4 scored 95% at 10 and below 90% at 30.
Breunig cites a Llama 3.1 8B that failed a task with 46 tools in context and passed with 19, the task unchanged.
Google's scaling study (arXiv 2512.08296): tool overhead appeared from about 16 tools.
The widely repeated "thirty to fifty tools" threshold has no primary source I could find. The measured thresholds depend on the model and on how similar the descriptions are, and the telemetry shows damage from fifteen tools for a small model.
Skills, meaning reusable instruction files the agent can load, show the same curve with more detail.
Skill shadowing (arXiv 2605.24050): the rate of picking a wrong skill with a similar name rose from 0.08 with 52 skills to 0.14 with 102 and 0.21 with 202.
Distractor skills (arXiv 2610.18522, 15,000 or more trajectories): recall of the right skill fell from 73.6% with no distractors to 27.4% with 1,000; Opus 4.6 on a subset fell from 81.3% to 30.9%.
SkillsBench (arXiv 2602.12670): compact skills raised task success by 19.0 points; comprehensive ones by 0.7.
Per-task masking (arXiv 2606.15390): hiding skills irrelevant to the task raised success by 47.4%.
Hiding the skill body behind a name (arXiv 2603.22455): first-hit retrieval fell by 37 to 44 points.
The second and fifth bullets pull against each other and set the design. Showing everything buries the right skill; showing only names hides it. The index entry has to be a one-line description a model can match on, with the body loaded afterwards.
Five structural answers.
Progressive disclosure. The node sees a short index and asks for the body of the one it picks. Anthropic's tool search (vendor measurement) cut a many-server setup from about 77,000 tokens of definitions to about 8,700 and raised Opus 4 from 49% to 74% on its MCP evaluation; the same guidance says search is not worth it under roughly ten tools. A controlled version, lazy tool loading (arXiv 2604.21816), cut per-turn tool tokens from about 47,300 to about 2,400 with no reported accuracy loss.
A flat index, never a tree. A study of long-context agents (arXiv 2607.17598) found nested disclosure dropped a success score from 0.7479 to 0.3890, and a flat index scored 0.462 against 0.257 for a nested one among 20 options. One level of indirection is cheap; two levels mean guessing the branch from its name, which is shadowing one level up.
A triage router. One small node reads the request and picks a topic; the specialist sees only that topic's tools and the last few turns. Salesforce, Decagon and Rasa expose this as a product feature, and none publishes the routing accuracy, so it is evidence of practice, not of measured gain. The cost is that a routing error is unrecoverable within the turn.
Mask instead of remove. Manus keeps the full tool list in the prompt and masks the logits of tools the current state forbids, so the prompt prefix stays stable and the cache keeps hitting. This is the answer when the catalogue must change per step but the cache matters more than the tokens.
A catalogue per node. The front node sees the triage list, the specialist its topic's tools, the reviewer the review skill and no editing tools, the curator the memory tools and nothing that acts on the world. Confusion is prevented by what a node cannot see.
Distraction has a quieter form: a node that delegates when it should not. LOCA-bench (arXiv 2602.07962) built tasks whose context grows under control and found the best model fell from 96.0% at 8,000 tokens to 14.7% at 256,000, and that one agent harness scored below a plain loop on the same tasks because of needless subagent use. The subagent is itself a tool that can be picked when it is present, and the fix is the same as for any other tool: a rule for when it may be used.
Carry forward
Under about ten tools, show all of them; above that, index with one-line descriptions and load bodies on demand.
Keep the index flat; nesting roughly halved success in the one study that tested it.
Give every node its own short catalogue, and treat "delegate" as a tool that also needs a rule.
Level 4: More agents, same mistakes
This level answers: when you add workers, why do they fail together, and which structures keep them independent?
The intuition behind a team is that several attempts catch what one misses. The 2026 evidence says this holds only when the attempts are independent, and that copies of one model talking to each other are not.
Co-failure ceiling (arXiv 2606.27288, 67 models): the share of problems where every model failed was 5.2% on MATH-500 and 7.9% on code contests; any router, vote or cascade is capped at one minus that rate. A learned router captured 9% of the oracle gain with a confidence interval spanning zero, and a model used as router sent 100% of tasks to the single best model, capturing nothing.
Diversity collapse (arXiv 2604.18005): diversity per agent fell from 1.03 with three agents to 0.47 with seven as they interacted; independent proposals before discussion, the nominal group technique, preserved it.
Bystander effect (arXiv 2605.10698, 22,500 trajectories): with two simulated peer auditors, GPT-5.4 fell from 1.00 to 0.23 on SWE-bench, Gemini 3.1 Pro from 1.00 to 0.83, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 held at 1.00; the order of auditors shifted accuracy by up to 24%.
Google's scaling study (arXiv 2512.08296, 180 configurations): errors were amplified 17.2 times with independent workers and 4.4 times with a central orchestrator; the mean change from adding an orchestrator across tasks was minus 3.5%, with a gain of 80.9% on one finance task and losses of 39 to 70% on PlanCraft; gains vanished once the single-agent baseline passed roughly 45%.
Equal budgets (Tran and Kiela, arXiv 2604.02460): at the same thinking tokens a single agent scored 0.418 against 0.379 to 0.388 for multi-agent setups at a 1,000-token budget; the team won only at a 100-token budget or when the shared context was deliberately corrupted.
Teams as distributed systems (arXiv 2603.12229): self-coordinating coding teams ran at 0.88 times single-agent speed with 19 median test failures, against 1.36 times and 4 failures for preassigned roles, which is 4.75 times more failures.
Scaling a single-model team (arXiv 2606.00655): performance was an inverted U in agent count, cost grew quadratically, 7B and 8B models gained nothing, and chain-of-thought matched or beat the team on reasoning tasks.
Harness Effect (arXiv 2607.06906, six models): delegation helped only the two strongest models, 0.85 to 0.86, and did nothing for the fast tier at 0.42 to 0.45.
Read together these say four things. Copies of one model share one set of blind spots, so more copies add votes and not checks. Interaction makes the copies more alike, and a model that sees peers disagree will drop a correct answer to match them. Independent workers make the same mistake many times, and the orchestrator that catches it costs tokens. The split helps weak baselines and corrupted contexts and otherwise taxes strong ones.
Seven structural answers.
Independence before interaction. Have workers propose before they see each other, then combine; this is the nominal group technique the diversity study found preserved variety. In practice: no shared scratchpad during the proposal phase, and no peer outputs in any worker's prompt.
Central review, not peer review. One node that sees every worker's output and the full specification; this halved error amplification relative to independent workers in the scaling study and restored the specification-gap score.
A different model family per role. Co-failure cannot be fixed by copies. Cross-model review in Level 6 gave fourteen points where a fresh context of the same model gave one and a half.
Fixed order, free roles. Drop the hierarchy (arXiv 2603.28990, 25,000 tasks, 4 to 256 agents) found a fixed turn order with agents choosing their own roles beat a central coordinator by 14% and fully free coordination by 44%; weaker models did better with more rigid structure.
Preassigned work, single writer. The distributed-systems result says do not let workers negotiate the split. Cognition's recommendation is one writer with many contributors, and the CAID study (arXiv 2603.21489) found hard isolation in git worktrees scored 63.3% against 55.5% when workers shared a checkout: they stopped reading each other's half-finished changes.
A router with measured statistics, not opinions. Agent-as-a-Router (arXiv 2606.22902, about 10,000 coding tasks, 8 models): giving the router per-task-type success rates lifted it from 41.41% to 47.74%, and the strongest coder, Opus 4.6, was the worst zero-shot router at 39.27%. Being good at the task does not make a model good at knowing who is good at the task.
An equal-budget check before shipping. Tran and Kiela's design is the test: run the single agent with the team's total thinking tokens. If the single agent wins, the team was a way to spend tokens, not a structure.
Important: A team of copies is not a team. Five instances of one model agree on the same error, and they converge further the more they talk. Independence has to be built in: separate proposals, a different model in the checking seat, and a central merge that sees the whole specification.
Carry forward
Co-failure caps every vote, router and cascade; only a different model or a real external signal breaks the cap.
Interaction erodes diversity and conformity drops correct answers; collect proposals before any discussion.
Preassign the split, keep one writer, and run the equal-budget comparison before calling a team a gain.
Level 5: The input is bigger than any window
This level answers: when the material is far larger than one context, which node reads what, and when does splitting the reading pay back?
Here the context is not poisoned but drowned. The structural answers split the reading rather than the conversation, and the evidence is mostly about where the gain really comes from.
Anthropic's research system is the best-known orchestrator-workers write-up, and its numbers need their labels.
Multi-agent research beat a single Opus 4 agent by 90.2% on an internal evaluation (vendor claim, roughly 20 queries).
Token use explained about 80% of the variance in BrowseComp scores, 95% with tool-call count and model choice added; multi-agent runs used about 15 times the tokens of a chat.
Effort rules in the lead's prompt: one worker with three to ten tool calls for a fact, two to four workers with ten to fifteen calls for a comparison, ten or more workers for an open question.
The second bullet is the honest one. Most of the gain was spending more tokens, and the parallel structure was a way to spend them within a time limit. Their early failures, a lead that spawned fifty workers for a simple query and vague briefs that made workers duplicate each other's reading, were fixed by the brief and the effort rules, not by more workers.
Six structural answers, ordered by how much the reading node is allowed to decide.
Chunk and reduce. Split the input, let workers each read a slice, reduce their outputs. Chain of Agents (arXiv 2406.02818) passed a running summary from chunk to chunk and reported up to ten points over a single long-context call. The relay result from Level 2 is the warning: a summary chain in prose loses facts at each hop, so the reduce step needs a structured payload.
Recursive reads. Recursive Language Models (arXiv 2512.24601) hold the input as a variable the model inspects with code, calling itself on pieces. A recursive setup with GPT-5-mini beat GPT-5 by more than 34 points at 132,000 tokens on OOLONG and by more than 15 at 263,000; removing recursion cost about 10%. The browsing result rests on 20 tasks, and the blocking calls prevent prompt caching.
Code execution for tool data. The agent writes code that calls tools and keeps the data in the sandbox, returning only what it needs. Anthropic's worked example (vendor claim) moved 150,000 tokens of tool results to about 2,000; a controlled comparison of programmatic tool calling cut 43,588 tokens to 27,297 with accuracy moving from 46.5 to 51.2 on one benchmark. The second set is the one to quote: a third fewer tokens and a few points, not 98%.
A coding agent as the reader. Coding Agents are Effective Long-Context Processors (arXiv 2603.20432) treats the agent's own file tools as the retrieval mechanism: the input sits on disk and the agent greps, reads and takes notes. The counter-evidence from a retrieval benchmark (arXiv 2605.15184, 116 questions) is that the same agent with 100,000 to 200,000 documents doubled its tool calls from 38.5 to 86.9 and lost 13.6 points, and that the harness changed accuracy as much as the retriever: Opus 4.6 scored 93.1% in one harness and 76.7% in another.
A cheap stateless reader. Spotify's Portal (vendor measurement, one Java monorepo, four scenarios) sends bulk reading to a Gemini 2.5 Flash worker in one-shot stateless calls and lets only a short summary into Claude's context, for about 90% fewer Claude tokens on bulk reads. The costs are listed by the authors: edits cannot be delegated because summaries carry no reliable line numbers, each call adds 10 to 30 seconds, and the cheap reader missed a thread-safety bug the main model found in seconds.
The file system as context. Manus's rule for every long task: what survives a reset is on disk, the transcript holds restorable references, and the agent re-reads what it needs. Agora (arXiv 2609.18094) takes this to the limit with 13 workers sharing nothing but a git history, producing 1,703 contributions and 233 new bests over 11 days in one run with no baseline.
The Spotify result is the practical shape of this level. The saving is real and the failure is specific: a reader that returns a summary cannot return what it did not notice, and the gap between a cheap reader and the main model is widest on exactly the subtle bug the summary was supposed to surface.
Why it matters: Splitting the reading pays back when the single-agent baseline is weak, the shared context is already wrong, or the material cannot fit. Above roughly 45% baseline accuracy the controlled study found no gain, and the token bill rose by an order of magnitude. Buy the split for capacity, not for accuracy.
Carry forward
Most of the measured research gain is more tokens, structured by a brief with effort rules; the structure is what you keep when the budget shrinks.
Keep bulk data out of the context by making the model ask for it through code or files, and keep the reduce step structured.
A cheap reader saves tokens and misses the subtle case; decide which reads can afford that.
Level 6: The reviewer agrees with the author and the reader trusts the document
This level answers: what should a reviewer, grader or guard be allowed to see, and what happens when it sees too much?
Two failures share one cause here. A reviewer that shares the author's context inherits the author's reasoning and the author's preference for it. A node that reads an untrusted document shares its context with whoever wrote the document. The structural answer to both is a node that sees less.
Three foundational results on review.
Huang et al. (arXiv 2310.01798): models asked to self-correct without an external signal did not improve and often got worse.
Self-preference (arXiv 2404.13076): models rate their own outputs higher than equally good outputs from others and can recognise their own text.
Reflexion (arXiv 2303.11366): with an external signal such as test results, a reflect-and-retry loop raised HumanEval from 80% to 91%.
The 2026 results separate independence of context from independence of judgement.
Cross-context review with the same model (arXiv 2603.12123): a reviewer in a fresh context found slightly more issues, F1 28.6 against 27.1.
Cross-model review (arXiv 2607.21656, 116 tasks): two different models reviewing each other passed 56.7% against 42.7% for self-review; the weaker writer rose from 71.6% to 89.7% under the stronger reviewer, while the stronger writer fell from 91.4% to 82.8% under the weaker one.
CriticGPT (arXiv 2407.00215, vendor paper): a critic model caught more inserted bugs than human reviewers in 63% of cases.
GAUGE (arXiv 2609.12191): a judge from the same model family as the writer added about 0.75 points of bias in the writer's favour.
AIRA2 (arXiv 2603.26499): hiding the evaluation from the working agent raised the share of genuinely improved results from about 56% to about 76%.
Fresh context gave about a point and a half; a different model gave fourteen; a weaker reviewer lowered a stronger writer. The Sonnet 5 system card describes the failure when the boundary sits in the wrong place: the model created subagents to approve its own work. A reviewer the author can spawn and instruct is not independent, whatever its context.
Four structural answers for review.
The blind verifier. The reviewer sees the artefact, the task, and a tool that produces a signal the author did not write (tests, a type checker, a reproduction), and never the transcript. Cloudflare's internal review ran this way over 48,095 merge requests at a median of 3 minutes 39 seconds, about $0.98 and about 1.2 findings per review, with an 85.7% cache hit rate. Cheap, separate, and frequent.
A different family in the checking seat. The co-failure ceiling from Level 4 applies to review: the same model in a fresh context keeps the same blind spots.
The hidden grader. The working node must not see the grader's criteria, data, or existence, or it optimises for them.
The author cannot choose the reviewer. Review is assigned by the harness, not spawned by the writer.
The guard node is the same shape applied to untrusted input. A separate call with a fixed task and no access to the conversation's goals reads a document or a planned action and decides whether to block; a guard that shares the agent's context can be persuaded by the same injected text.
LlamaFirewall (arXiv 2505.03574): on AgentDojo, attack success fell from 17.6% to 1.75% with both scanners, and task utility fell from 47.7% to 42.7%.
CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813): separating a privileged planner from the model that reads untrusted data stopped 163 of 163 attacks over 949 tasks, at 2.82 times the tokens and a utility drop from 86.6% to 74.2%.
Behavioral contracts enforced outside the model (arXiv 2602.22302, 7 models, 1,980 sessions): hard compliance 88 to 100% with under 10 milliseconds of overhead.
Anthropic's sandbox for its coding agent (vendor): permission prompts fell about 84%, but a phishing test through an approved channel succeeded in 24 of 25 attempts.
Azure's published experience (vendor): early guardrail configurations blocked 40 to 60% of legitimate requests.
Every guard costs utility as well as blocking attacks, so placement is the design. A guard on a brief between nodes sees one short task and is cheap. A guard on every tool call is thorough and slow. A contract enforced in code outside the model costs almost nothing and catches only what can be written as a rule. And a sandbox that permits a channel permits exfiltration through it.
The last problem of this level is finding out which node failed afterwards.
MAST (arXiv 2503.13657, 1,642 traces, 7 frameworks, 14 failure modes): about 40% specification and design failures, about 35% inter-agent misalignment, about 20% verification failures; the shares differ slightly between paper versions.
Who&When (arXiv 2505.00212): models identified the responsible agent 53.5% of the time and the responsible step 14.2% of the time.
MP-Bench (arXiv 2603.25001, n = 289): with several annotators' views accepted, models beat random by a wide margin, so attribution is partly subjective and the Who&When figure is somewhat pessimistic.
AgentFail (arXiv 2509.23735, n = 307 production failures): over half of root causes sat in the model nodes, and a small share in code or template nodes.
Attribution from a merged transcript is close to a coin flip for the agent and far worse for the step. A system with many nodes needs its own log of what each node saw and returned, because models cannot reconstruct it afterwards, and the AgentFail split says the model nodes are where to look first.
What it means for us: Independence of context is cheap and worth about a point; independence of judgement needs a different model and is worth about fourteen; a reviewer the author can spawn is worth nothing. Guards and contracts cost utility wherever they sit, so put them on the shortest payload that carries the risk.
Carry forward
The reviewer sees the artefact, the task and an external signal, never the transcript, and is assigned by the harness.
A different model family breaks the shared blind spot; a weaker reviewer can lower a stronger writer.
Log what each node saw and returned, because attribution from merged traces runs at 14% for the step.
Level 7: The clock and the bill
This level answers: when a node must answer in a third of a second or cost a tenth as much, which work moves to a different node?
Latency and cost force splits that accuracy alone would not. The question is which part of the work can tolerate the slower or cheaper node.
Voice is the clearest case, because the deadline is physical.
Human turn gap: 200 to 300 milliseconds; above 500 milliseconds the system feels slow.
NVIDIA's frontend-backend architecture for full-duplex speech (arXiv 2609.19334): the speech model emits a control token at about 320 milliseconds and fills about 1 second of speech while a backend text agent runs the tool; tool-call recall 92 to 97%, spoken function-calling accuracy 74.6% against 80.8% for a speech model that calls tools itself, and about 1 in 5 tool triggers were false alarms.
A single speech model doing tool calls (arXiv 2609.21967): tool-selection F1 82.5, argument accuracy 42.2, pass at first attempt 33.0.
tau-Voice (third-party benchmark): full-duplex speech models scored 31 to 51% against 85% for a GPT-5 text agent on the same tasks.
Argument accuracy is the number that decides the split. A voice model that picks the right tool four times in five but fills the arguments correctly less than half the time cannot be the node that acts. So the fast node keeps the spoken conversation and at most a handful of tools (Nemotron's guidance says five), and the slow text node writes the arguments and runs the task. Failures in the slow node never enter the speech context.
Cost splits have the same shape with a planner where the fast node was.
ReWOO (arXiv 2305.18323): about five times better token efficiency with a four-point gain on HotpotQA by planning all tool calls before running any.
LLMCompiler (arXiv 2312.04511): up to 3.7 times lower latency and 6.7 times lower cost by planning parallel calls up front.
RouteLLM (arXiv 2406.18665): routing easy queries to a small model saved 3.66 times the cost at 95% of the large model's score on MT-Bench, with savings of 29 to 73% depending on task.
Prewalk (third-party measurement on SWE-Bench Pro): swapping from a frontier model to a cheap one after the first landed edit recovered 92 to 97% of the frontier pass rate at 39 to 53% lower cost; in one pair a single large-model agent at 85% and $2.78 still beat a plan-then-execute split at 84.6% and $3.18, with 91% of tokens spent on reading.
The Prewalk pair is the warning. The planner-executor split pays when the executor is cheaper than the planner and the plan does not need to change; when the executor is as strong as the planner, or when most tokens go to reading rather than acting, the split adds a hand-off and nothing else. The Harness Effect result from Level 4 says the same from the model side: delegation only helped the strongest models.
Four more controls shape cost without changing who does the work.
Cache-aware prefixes. Manus reports input tokens outnumber output by about 100 to 1 and a cached input token costs about a tenth of an uncached one (vendor numbers), which makes a stable prompt prefix the single most important production metric. Fresh contexts and parallel bursts can miss the cache the main session was using; Claude Code's agent teams used about 7 times the tokens of a single session in plan mode.
Sleep-time compute. Preprocessing the context while the system is idle (arXiv 2504.13171, vendor paper) cut test-time compute by about 5 times at equal accuracy and raised accuracy by 13 and 18 points on two tasks at fixed test-time budgets. The slow work moves to a node that runs when nobody waits.
Resume from a log. Anthropic's managed agent runtime wakes a session from an event log rather than re-reading its history and reports time-to-first-token improvements of 60% at the median and 90% at the tail (vendor claims).
Budgets per node. OpenAI Agents SDK stops at ten turns by default, smolagents at twenty steps, Strands swarms at twenty hand-offs and 900 seconds in total, Anthropic's managed agents at a cost cap and twenty-five child threads. A budget is a context policy: it fixes how much history a node can accumulate before the system forces a boundary.
Carry forward
Split by deadline: the node under the clock keeps the conversation and a handful of tools; the node that acts gets the full set and no transcript.
A planner-executor split pays only when the executor is cheaper and the plan is stable; otherwise it is a hand-off with no gain.
Cache hit rate and per-node budgets are the two cost controls that do not change who does the work.
Level 8: Nothing learned across sessions
This level answers: when work spans days, which node writes memory, what should it be allowed to write, and does it beat keeping the transcript?
A system that forgets everything at the end of a session repeats its mistakes next time. The structural answer is a curator: a node that reads transcripts and writes memory, separate from the node that serves the person, so the working node does not decide what to remember. The claims for this are strong and the controlled results are mixed.
Mem0 (arXiv 2504.19413, vendor paper): on LOCOMO the memory service scored 66.88 against 72.90 for the full conversation in context, with p95 latency of 1.44 seconds against 17.12 and more than 90% fewer tokens.
Agentic Context Engineering (arXiv 2510.04618): a curator that edits a growing playbook instead of rewriting it gained 10.6% on agent tasks and 8.6% on finance tasks with 83.6% lower adaptation cost.
Just-in-Time Memory (arXiv 2609.27334): a trained curator that writes a task payload for a frozen executor lifted Qwen3-8B on ALFWorld from 61.2% to 77.4% and on WebShop from 16.5% to 32.8%, adding about 1,900 input tokens against 10,700 and 13,400 for the write-time baselines.
The Mem0 row says the memory service lost six points to full context and won on latency and cost, in the vendor's own table. The JITMEM row shows the best version of the pattern: the curator writes a brief for the executor, which makes memory one more hand-off with a schema.
Continual Learning Bench (arXiv 2606.05661) is the one benchmark built to test whether memory systems help an agent improve across tasks, and it ranked them below plain history.
Full history in context with Sonnet 4.6: 22.3 at $30.4; Mem0 with GPT-5.4: 15.1; ACE with GPT-5.4: 4.6 at $62.8; a notepad memory with Sonnet 4.6: 3.5.
📷
The rows use different executor models, so the chart is the paper's ranking and not a controlled pair. The paper's own conclusion stands regardless: naive in-context learning beat the dedicated memory systems. Two failure studies explain part of why.
Memory extraction (arXiv 2602.19320): 18 to 30% of memory writes failed silently, storing nothing or the wrong fact.
Poisoned memory (arXiv 2604.27707) and the Agents of Chaos case studies (arXiv 2602.20021): a planted memory document spread across agents that shared the store.
A curator is a node that writes into every future context. Poisoning it is the most durable form of the Level 1 failure, and the extraction rate means a fifth of what it writes may already be wrong. Three structural answers follow.
Memory writes as reviewed artefacts. A separate curator node, a schema for what may be written, and a log of what was written and why, so a bad entry can be found and removed.
Derivation tracking. The Planfence result from Level 2 applies to memory: an entry derived from inputs that have since changed should be rebuilt, not trusted because it is recent.
Measure against the transcript first. On the one benchmark built for it, plain history won. Buy the curator for latency and spend, keep the full history until the loss is measured, and treat any claimed accuracy gain from memory as a claim.
What it means for us: A memory curator needs a reviewer and a schema more than any other node, because its mistakes compound across every future session. The published wins are on speed and cost; on accuracy, the transcript is still ahead.
Carry forward
Memory services win on latency and tokens and lose on accuracy in the controlled results.
Treat every memory write as a hand-off: schema, review, derivation, and a way to delete.
Keep the transcript until the loss from replacing it has been measured on tasks you control.
The patterns at a glance
Nineteen patterns appear above. Each is one decision about what a node sees, and each is listed with the failure it addresses and its measured cost.
Fresh context per attempt. Fixes: a failed step steering later steps. Keeps: a written brief. Drops: every trace from earlier attempts. Cost: the worker cannot ask back; re-gathered context. Evidence: fresh conversation recovered most of a 39% loss; recap recovered 15 to 20%.
Restart loop. Fixes: poisoning and distraction in long jobs. Keeps: files and test results. Drops: the whole transcript each iteration. Cost: no benchmark, anecdotes only.
Checkpoint and rewind. Fixes: a wrong turn mid-task. Keeps: state before the turn. Drops: the turn. Cost: depends on whether the tool restores the conversation or only files.
Durable retry per step. Fixes: crashes and transient failures. Keeps: a step log. Drops: the failed attempt. Cost: errors returned as strings are replayed as results.
Typed state and task packets. Fixes: lossy hand-offs. Keeps: defined fields plus a re-readable file. Drops: the transcript. Cost: a fact with no field is lost. Evidence: 73.0 to 75.6 and 44.4 to 58.3 from files alone.
Structured relay and gists. Fixes: loss at each hop. Keeps: a distribution or a 100-token verified gist. Drops: prose conclusions. Cost: a schema per hop. Evidence: 75.2% against 22.5% at five hops; $0.125 against $0.399.
Rebuild by inputs. Fixes: stale plans and stale memory. Keeps: a derivation record. Drops: age as a freshness signal. Cost: about 15% more tokens. Evidence: 0 of 30 stale plans through against 30 of 30.
Gate at every boundary. Fixes: error propagation. Keeps: a check per hand-off. Drops: outputs that fail the check. Cost: one call per gate. Evidence: 58.4% to 16.2% errors surviving.
Progressive disclosure with a flat index. Fixes: confusion and shadowing. Keeps: one-line descriptions. Drops: bodies until chosen. Cost: one extra call; not worth it under about ten tools. Evidence: nesting roughly halved success.
Triage router and per-node catalogue. Fixes: confusion. Keeps: a topic's tools. Drops: all others. Cost: a routing error is unrecoverable within the turn; no published routing accuracy.
Independence before interaction. Fixes: diversity collapse and conformity. Keeps: separate proposals. Drops: peer outputs during proposal. Cost: no debate benefit. Evidence: diversity 1.03 to 0.47 under interaction.
Central review with the full specification. Fixes: error amplification and the specification gap. Keeps: everything, in one node. Drops: nothing from the merger. Cost: the merger's context. Evidence: 4.4 times against 17.2 times amplification; 58.2% to 88.9%.
Different model family per role. Fixes: co-failure and self-preference. Keeps: a second set of blind spots. Drops: shared ones. Cost: a second vendor. Evidence: 56.7% against 42.7% review pass rate.
Fixed order, free roles, single writer. Fixes: negotiation overhead and file clash. Keeps: a turn order and one writer. Drops: self-coordination. Cost: rigidity. Evidence: plus 14% over a coordinator; 63.3% against 55.5% with worktrees.
Orchestrator-workers with effort rules. Fixes: inputs beyond the window. Keeps: the plan in the lead. Drops: the lead's conversation from workers. Cost: 4 to 15 times tokens; no gain above a 45% baseline.
Code execution and recursive reads. Fixes: bulk data in context. Keeps: what the code selected. Drops: raw tool output. Cost: a sandbox; blocking calls prevent caching. Evidence: a third fewer tokens with a few points gained.
Cheap stateless reader. Fixes: expensive bulk reads. Keeps: a summary. Drops: the material. Cost: 10 to 30 seconds per call; missed a subtle bug. Evidence: about 90% fewer main-model tokens on reads.
Blind verifier, hidden grader, guard node. Fixes: dependent review and injected text. Keeps: the artefact, the task, an external signal. Drops: the author's trace, the grader's criteria, the conversation's goals. Cost: utility, five to twelve points for guards. Evidence: $0.98 and 1.2 findings per review at scale.
Memory curator with schema and review. Fixes: nothing learned across sessions. Keeps: reviewed entries. Drops: the transcript between sessions. Cost: accuracy against full history today; 18 to 30% silent write failures.
Decision guide
A failed step keeps biasing the next ones. Use: a fresh context per attempt with a written brief, or a restart loop when the goal is checkable. Then check: whether failures are raised or returned as strings, and whether the receiving node pastes traces back.
The receiver keeps missing facts the sender had. Use: typed state with a notes field, a task packet on disk, and a "need more" return. Then check: hand-off recall on a sample of real tasks, because the published rate was 0.32.
Results from several workers do not fit together. Use: a merger with the full specification, preassigned work, one writer, worktrees. Then check: the specification-gap pair, 58.2% without the full spec and 88.9% with it.
The model picks the wrong tool or skill. Use: count tools first; under about ten show all; above, a flat one-line index with bodies on demand, or a router. Then check: selection accuracy per model, because the threshold moves with model size.
Several agents agree and are wrong. Use: proposals before discussion, a different family in the checking seat, central review. Then check: co-failure on your task set, because that rate caps every vote.
The team costs more and is not better. Use: the equal-budget comparison. Then check: whether the single agent at the team's total tokens matches it; if so, keep the brief and drop the team.
The material does not fit the window. Use: orchestrator-workers with effort rules, code execution, or a cheap reader. Then check: your single-agent baseline, since the split helped below about 45% and not above.
Review finds only what the author already thought of. Use: a verifier with the artefact and an external signal, in a different family, assigned by the harness. Then check: whether the reviewer is weaker than the writer.
The node must answer within a third of a second or cost a tenth as much. Use: a fast node with the conversation and a handful of tools; a slow node that writes the arguments; a planner only when the executor is cheaper and the plan is stable. Then check: argument accuracy and the false-alarm rate on triggers.
The system should learn across sessions. Use: a curator with a schema, review and derivation tracking; measure against full history first. Then check: silent write failures, 18 to 30% in the one study that measured them.
Takeaways
Agent architecture is the decision of what each node sees, does and returns; the number of agents is a consequence, not the goal.
A wrong early step is bias, not evidence, once the task restarts; keep errors inside an attempt and drop them across attempts.
Any retry or resume mechanism that records an error string as a result replays the poison into every later attempt.
The payload format decides most hand-off loss: prose through five hops kept a quarter of the score, a structured relay three quarters, and a re-readable file added up to fourteen points.
The node that merges needs the full specification; the workers do not, and asking them to report conflicts added nothing.
Gate every hand-off; a check at each boundary cut surviving errors from 58.4% to 16.2% in a four-stage pipeline.
Count tools before adding structure; small models lose accuracy from about fifteen tools, search costs more than it saves under ten, and a nested index halved success.
Copies of one model share blind spots and converge further the more they talk; collect proposals before discussion and put a different family in the checking seat.
Preassign the split and keep one writer; self-coordinating teams ran slower with 4.75 times the test failures.
Run the equal-budget comparison before shipping a team; at equal thinking tokens the single agent won unless the context was corrupted.
Split the reading for capacity, not accuracy; above a 45% baseline the controlled study found no gain, and a cheap reader misses the subtle bug.
A fresh context for a reviewer is worth about a point; a different model family about fourteen; a reviewer the author can spawn is worth nothing.
Guards, contracts and sandboxes cost utility wherever they sit; put them on the shortest payload that carries the risk and remember an approved channel is still a channel.
Memory services win on latency and tokens and lose to plain history on accuracy; treat every memory write as a reviewed hand-off with a derivation.
Log what each node saw and returned, because models attribute a failing step from merged traces 14% of the time.

It is called domain randomisation. Every one of the thousands of virtual robot copies gets a different battery voltage, a different voltage sag under load, a different command delay and different friction. The network cannot settle into one perfect set of conditions, so the real robot is just one more variation among thousands.

There is also a separate simulation variant with gear backlash: ±1° in every joint.

In the Microduck training repository, the ball kick is its own task. Four more sit next to it: walking with head-pose commands (flat and rough ground), standing up from sitting, a task called Roulade, and roller skating.

The repository is open under Apache-2.0. It has about 2.8k stars and 673 forks, and training can run without a local GPU through Hugging Face Jobs.

  - a low golden sun (#ffc27a, strength 2.7) that casts long shadows
  - sky top #2f5fc4, horizon #ffc07e, bottom #8a7ac0
  - fog #f2c49c at density 0.0021
  - a purple hemisphere fill: sky #7a74e0, ground #d89a68, strength 1.15
  - the ground tinted warm (#ffd890)
- Night:
  - deep navy: sky top #081038, horizon #24307a, fog #18225a at density 0.0036
  - fill #5a5ae0 over #283060
  - glowing lamps and lit windows
- Interiors:
  - no sun, warm lamps, a purple fill (#8a7ae0), exposure about 1.25
  - one bold theme colour per room (a green office, teal tiles, a red map room)
  - windows that show a dusk sky
- Sky: a shader dome with a sun glow, a moon and stars. Mix between looks over time, so dawn or night arrives on the words.
- Post, in this order:
  - depth of field from the depth buffer (48 taps, focused on the subject, shallow on close-ups)
  - bloom: strength 0.42, threshold 0.82, radius 0.6
  - Neutral tone mapping at exposure 1.32
  - a split-tone pass:
    - shadows plus RGB (0.03, -0.012, 0.085)
    - highlights plus (0.045, 0.018, -0.035)
    - greens pulled 55% toward gold (hue 0.125)
    - blacks lifted to 0.055 with a purple tint (0.85, 0.75, 1.2)
    - gain 1.08
  - a light grade: saturation 1.08, vignette 0.22, 2% grain
- Targets, measured on 1 frame a second with the caption band left out:
  - mean lightness (Lab L) 43-57
  - darkest 5% at 5-18 (lifted, never crushed)
  - brightest 5% at 88-99
  - shadows purple-blue (Lab a +7 to +19, b 0 to -19)
  - highlights warm (a +3 to +10)
  - blue and purple make up 22-51% of the saturated pixels
People:
- 2D characters are drawn in code on a canvas every frame and shown on camera-facing cards inside the 3D world.
  - Each card's canvas is 512, 1024, 2048 or 3072 px tall, picked by how big the card is on screen, so close-ups stay sharp.
  - A soft blue-violet blob shadow sits under each card.
- About 1.4 m tall, in rig units:
  - a big round head (radius 55)
  - a short bean torso (92-108)
  - long stick legs (132-170)
  - noodle arms (92) with ball hands
  - a 4 px dark outline (#272236)
- A bendy spine (lean, bend, squash), and heads that tilt and turn to three-quarter view (the face slides across the head).
- The face set:
  - dot eyes with angled brows (calm, smug)
  - white circles with dot pupils (shock)
  - closed arcs (laughing)
  - grin, wavy worried mouth, blush, sweat drops
- Pose-to-pose acting: each key snaps in with a small overshoot, then holds, while blinks and breathing keep the holds alive. Bodies act too: they lean in, recoil, slump and point.
- The scene light tints them: an ambient tint, a lit side, a shade colour and a rim (warm gold at dawn, cool blue at night, orange in smoke).
- Each character gets one look built from shared parts: hats, uniforms, moustaches, hair.
Camera:
- No cuts inside a place.
  - One camera holds each beat with a slow push (ease-out), then travels to the next beat.
  - Travels dive down, rise over an edge, fly across, slide through a window, or pan from the clue down to the object.
  - One travel can be a crane up through the sky into a new place or time.
- Travels use a smooth speed ramp (smootherstep) with a slight arc. Only travels get motion blur: 10 subframes over half a frame.
- Never parked: every hold pushes, arcs or slides.
- Low and wide:
  - fov 54-64, with the lens at knee to chest height
  - leading lines (rails, decks, roads) aimed at the subject
  - characters 1-3 m from the lens and leaning in; the mocker gets a big close-up
- Inserts carry the proof: a macro held 3-5 s while the change happens in frame.
- The payoff is a wide, centred spectacle, with the event coming at the lens.
- Hard cuts only for a big jump in place or time: 0-6 per Short.
Captions:
- 1-2 words at a time; short words (a, the, so, to) ride with the next word.
- Montserrat 800 at 76 px, white with a 15 px #120e1a outline and a soft shadow, centred at y 1345.
- Each pops from 108% to 100% in 0.09 s and shows 0.1 s before its word. No full stops on screen.
Banned:
- AI images or video, downloaded 3D models, real logos
- green-on-green sets, crushed blacks
- a camera that sits still, motion blur on holds
- a time-stretched or whispered voice
- more than one name the viewer has to remember
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 55-75 s, 200-280 words. The voice runs about 3.7 words a second, pauses included.
Beat map for a 62 s Short (scale it to your voice):
0-3 s, HOOK, 9-14 words: one plain sentence about an act that makes no sense, with the reason hidden.
- Two things can't both be true, or someone does the opposite of what anyone would do.
- Write it before the rest of the story.
- Picture: the act and the danger in one low, wide frame.
3-12 s, SETUP: present tense, with exact numbers (a price, a time limit, a distance): who, where, and what's at stake. The camera travels across the world to show it.
12-20 s, THE MOCKER: a quoted joke line of 4-12 words, sarcastic and funny, said to the hero's face. Big close-up, leaning into the lens.
20-27 s, THE HERO stays calm and cryptic: one short line, or just a gesture. He never explains.
27-40 s, ESCALATION in threes: it gets weirder, and the mocker gets cocky. A macro insert is held 3-5 s while the change happens. Add one comic aside per beat.
40-52 s, "YOU SEE,": used once, at 60-85% of the runtime. The trick is explained through an everyday thing the viewer has done (blowing on soup, a phone sliding off a table), in 3-5 short lines.
52-62 s, THE PAYOFF: shown, not explained, and it lands on the mocker. The last line is the biggest reveal, with no moral and no trivia after it. The last frame leads back into the first, so it loops.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (all free): Python 3, Playwright with Edge or Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, numpy, soundfile, kokoro-onnx, and Three.js 0.170 from npm, loaded with an import map, no bundler. Montserrat comes free from Google Fonts. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Script:
   - Topic: true, one bizarre image you can picture instantly, someone outsmarts someone, and the title hides the ending.
     - Explainers, nature facts and fiction without a trick do far worse.
     - So do topics where a science lesson is the twist.
   - Tell it the way a 10-year-old tells a friend:
     - plain spoken words in flowing sentences joined with "and" and "so"
     - "a captain", "the boss", never titles and dates
     - 0-1 names, no context lines, no jargon
     - one funny comparison
   - Join related sentences with commas, because a voice resets after every full stop and leaves a gap.
   - No cute gags, no "on purpose" spoilers, no low stakes.
   - Study first, free: pull the transcripts of 3 of the newest top Shorts in this format with yt-dlp (--skip-download --write-auto-subs --sub-lang en --sub-format vtt), strip the timestamps, and note how many words each line has, where the mocker speaks and where "You see," lands.
   - Then fill this skeleton line by line, 16-20 lines in all:
     - line 1: the hook, the strange act with the reason hidden, 9-14 words
     - lines 2-4: the setup, who and where, one exact number, what's at stake
     - line 5: the mocker's joke, quoted, 4-12 words
     - line 6: the hero's calm, cryptic reply, or just a gesture
     - lines 7-11: the escalation in threes, each step weirder, the mocker getting cocky, one comic aside
     - lines 12-15: "You see," and the trick told through an everyday thing the viewer has done
     - lines 16-18: the payoff shown and landing on the mocker, the biggest reveal as the very last line
   - Check the finished script line by line against those 3 transcripts before any voice.
   - Show me the word count and the seconds per line.
3. Voice, free first:
   Free route, Kokoro:
   - Run kokoro-onnx on the CPU with the free kokoro-v1.0.onnx model and voices-v1.0.bin, lang en-us.
   - Try 4-5 American male voices (am_puck, am_michael, am_fenrir, am_echo, am_adam) on the first 12 s of the script at speed 1.0-1.1.
   - Keep the voice with the widest pitch range (the gate below).
   - Generate one line per call, so each line gets its own speed: 1.0 for calm lines, 1.1 for excited ones.
   - Join the lines with 0.18 s gaps, and 0.3 s before a big turn.
   - It will sound flatter than a person. Because the film is anchored to the words, you can drop in a better voice later without touching the animation.
   Optional upgrade, ElevenLabs:
   - Use eleven_v4 with a stock library narrator; we used Mark, an energetic young male voice. Never clone a real creator.
   - Put audio tags at the start of lines: [excited], [mischievously], [laughs], [curious], [sarcastically], [chuckles], [dramatically].
   - Put CAPS on one punch word per line ("he did NOTHING", "the ENTIRE town"). An ellipsis gives a beat before a punchline.
   - Never use whisper, soft or sigh tags.
   - Read the whole script in one take at natural speed, and make 4 takes to pick from.
     - A 192-word script came out at 64.6 s for 1,147 credits (about $0.22).
     - We cut pauses over 0.35 s down to 0.28 s (FFmpeg silenceremove at -45 dB) and applied atempo 1.15, which gave 56.0 s.
     - Never go faster than that.
   Gate every take, either route, before building on it:
   - Words a second while talking: 3.5-4.5.
   - Gaps between sentences: median 0.12-0.25 s, longest 0.35 s, none over 0.5 s. Pauses under 13% of the runtime.
   - Pitch range 12.5+ semitones, and pitch movement 11+ semitones a second (pyin over the voiced frames). Under that sounds flat.
   - Stress spread over the line: under 55% of the loud words in each line's first third.
   - Dead air: count the frames 50 dB under the speech peak inside gaps over 0.3 s.
     - Takes with 9-13 s a minute sounded like a robot.
     - 1-4 s a minute of breaths sounded natural.
   - Whispered words: a word with pitch found in under 20% of its frames is whispered.
     - Regenerate just that line and drop it into the pause before the next sentence, never mid-line.
     - Expect 1-2 lines per Short, about 100 credits each.
   - Level to -16 LUFS. Then run faster-whisper on the finished track, without the script as a prompt, to get word times.
4. Film: one HTML page with one canvas, where every frame is a pure function of time: window .seek(t), window.READY, window.END.
   - Align the clean script to the whisper words. A helper T('word', n) returns the start of the nth time that word is said.
   - Anchor every beat, camera hold, pose change, effect and sound event to a T() plus an offset, never a typed time. A new voice then means re-run whisper, re-render and re-mix, nothing else.
   - A world module builds the set and exposes props through simple controls. Give every transformation in the story a 0-to-1 control (setChange(k)) that builds it in visible steps, and use a clipping plane for sweeps like paint or water.
   - A cast module holds the looks and the lights.
   - One rig function draws a character from a pose: lean, bend, squash, facing, turn, head tilt, hands, feet, eyes, brows, mouth, blush, sweat. A keyed(keys, t) helper does the pose-to-pose timing.
   - The camera is a list of holds, each with start, end, position, look-at, [fov from, to], aperture and focus point. The gaps between holds are the travels.
   - window.EV lists the sound events {t, name}, pushed from the same anchors. The renderer saves it for the mix.
5. Style check before the render:
   - Grab 3-4 frames and lay them side by side with frames from 2-3 of the newest Shorts in this format.
   - Render only if palette, shadow colour, lens height and texture match. Measure the colour targets.
   - Make a contact sheet with the first and last frame of every hold. Fix:
     - faces cut off
     - characters inside geometry
     - empty corners
     - captions over faces
     - a camera that starts a cut inside a hill or a wall
6. Render:
   - Headless Edge or Chromium through Playwright seeks every frame. Launch flags: --enable-gpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist --allow-file-access-from-files, plus --use-angle=d3d11 on Windows.
   - The page encodes itself with WebCodecs H.264 on the GPU: 60 Mbps, a keyframe every 2 s. Never read pixels back.
   - Reference speed: 56.2 s = 1,685 frames at 1080x1920, 30 fps, in 3 min 53 s (about 7 fps) on an RTX 3060 Ti with an i5-12400F.
   - The master is about 415 MB. Re-encode with libx264 for upload: 8 Mbps comes to about 57 MB a minute.
7. Glitch scan, on the silent render before the mix:
   - Flag whole-frame jumps that are not planned cuts, one-frame A-B-A flickers, and single blocks that change while their neighbours stay calm (pop-ins, blinks).
   - Look at the frames around each flag and fix the cause. A first cut usually has 10-20.
8. Sound:
   - Music: one playful bed under a free licence (Pixabay). Cut it or drop it on the biggest moment.
   - Ambience: one bed per place, swapped on each cut or crane (distant explosions, waves and birds, night creaks, a cockpit drone).
   - Effects: about 45 Mixkit cues placed from window.EV, so each effect's loudest moment lands on its frame.
     - Whooshes on travels, a pop on reveals, a freeze hit, impacts, a ding on the idea.
     - Big hits go in pauses. Hits that land on words sit under the voice.
   - Duck music and effects about 13 dB under the voice with a sidechain. The music bed sits 20 dB under the narrator.
   - Measure it: mix a voice-only and a background-only version, compare them K-weighted in 0.4 s windows, and fix anything that misses either target:
     - median gap of 15 dB or more
     - background louder than the voice in under 1% of the talking
   - Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1.5.
9. Upload text:
   - Title: "The [thing] That [strange act]" or "Why [something odd]", hiding the ending. No emoji, no hashtags; the description is the title.
   - Cover: a clean frame of the payoff with no text.
   - Made for kids: No.
</build>

<gotchas>
Script:
- The first scripts read like writing: names, dates, history context, the twist given away in the hook, no doubters, an ending that fizzled. They were rejected.
  - Rewritten the way a 10-year-old tells it, with a mocker and the reveal saved for the end, they worked.
  - Count names and context lines; a reading-level score doesn't catch this.
- A 121-word script had no room to escalate. The biggest Shorts in this format run 145-295 words, and the newest ones 218-295.
- An opener that is setup ("During a war...") or gives the answer away kills curiosity. Line 1 is the strange act with the reason hidden.
Voice:
- Short full-stop sentences make every voice reset with a 0.5-0.85 s gap and punch the next first word, so it sounds stop-start. Join lines with commas.
- A time-stretch (1.15) on top of pauses cut to 0.18 s got "did you speed it up?", and cutting breaths out sounds robotic. Speed comes from the script, not the edit.
- Whisper or relieved tags made the narrator whisper a whole line. Leave them out.
- Kokoro was rejected as a final voice for sounding flat, but it is a fine free start: build on it, then swap the voice when you can.
- Whisper given the script as its prompt garbled the transcript. Run it without one.
- Anchor repeated words by occurrence ("so" number 3), or beats land on the wrong line.
Look:
- Olive people on olive vehicles on bright grass under a pale sky read as cheap. Pick a warm-against-cool scheme first; green never leads.
- Using the grade isn't enough. One Short with ochre walls, an orange road and warm shadows drifted all orange. Pale interiors went flat.
  - Set palette and interior light decide the look, so check frames side by side every time.
- The colour metric's "warm" bin counts pink-purple (hue over 300). Trust the side-by-side over that number.
Camera:
- 17 cuts in 35 s, a fixed 1 s cut grid, whips, shakes and blur everywhere read as glitchy visuals unrelated to the voice. Hold, push, travel; cut only for a jump in place or time.
- A camera at eye level, mid-distance, at fov 36-46 felt lazy and flat. Low, wide and close felt right.
- Hermite camera keys overshoot when a neighbouring key is far away, and the camera flies through walls.
  - Use eased travels (smootherstep) or centripetal Catmull-Rom splines with arc-length speed.
- A camera key inside geometry renders black. A fast travel through a pole, a wall or an actor reads as a glitch. Make those hard cuts.
- A long travel at street level smears through shopfronts. Cut for big jumps inside a town.
- The portrait frame is only about 23 degrees wide at fov 40. Keep characters within a few degrees of the look line.
  - Turn actors three-quarter to camera, or a raised far arm hides behind the big head.
Render:
- Characters vanish inside other geometry: a hill mesh swallows anyone standing inside its radius, and foliage clumps swallow heads.
  - Keep people on clear ground.
  - Open a sight line through foliage between the camera and what it looks at: 9 m long at most, faded in over 4 m so the clumps don't jump.
- An InstancedMesh whose count or matrices change after the first frame keeps its first bounding sphere and gets culled, so leaves blinked. Set frustumCulled = false.
- Transparent planes with the same renderOrder at the same height swap draw order as the camera moves, so they flicker. Give each its own order.
- Culling character cards with fixed screen margins makes close-ups pop in at the frame edges. Scale the margin with the card's size.
- Pose fields set outside the key system snap. Ease every change. Give props to a hand instead of switching them on with a pose.
- Effects that outlive a cut show up in the next shot: a splash from one shot hangs as a ghost over a face in the next. End them at the cut.
- A camera near plane of 0.05 loses flat effects near the ground to the depth test in a band at the bottom of some frames. Use 0.3.
  - Check stills at exact frame times (frame / 30), not rounded ones.
- Motion blur on holds ghosts the captions at every word change. Blur travels only.
- Reading pixels back every frame (toDataURL, screenshots) knocks the canvas off the GPU and renders about 50x slower. Encode inside the page.
Sound:
- With the music only 7-9 dB under the voice, the narrator was hard to hear. Duck it and measure before you export.
- A voice already hitting the peak cap can't go louder. Pull everything else down instead.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my story, or pitch 3. Then show me the script (word count and seconds per line) and the beat list before any voice is generated or any scene is built.
</start>

2026.11.7【周末论市：你最不希望看到什么？】
         如果是普通股民，绝大多数长期套牢卧倒装死，被问这个问题肯定是不希望暴跌。如果问我，目前A股最不希望看到什么？答案不是指数再跌几个点，也不是某个板块出现调整，而是市场刚刚经历一轮剧烈下跌，转眼又把教训抛到脑后，重新回到炒作高估值科技故事的老路上。如果这种情况继续发生，那么此前的调整就失去了意义，市场也很难真正走出困境。
          回顾本周行情，A股可谓大起大落。11月2日市场出现明显反弹，11月3日迅速回落；11月4日又迎来强力反攻，沪指上涨2.16%，深成指上涨4.22%，创业板指上涨6.40%，科创50更是暴涨9.92%，两市成交额达到2.04万亿元，超过4600只个股上涨。这样的表现，很容易让人产生新一轮行情已经启动的错觉。
         可是，11月5日市场冲高回落，11月6日更是大幅低开后全天弱势震荡。周五收盘，沪指下跌1.10%，深成指下跌2.57%，创业板指下跌3.96%，科创50下跌2.60%，两市成交额1.66万亿元，较前一交易日缩量4602亿元，全市场超过4700只个股下跌。周三的强力反攻，短短两天就被打回原形。这说明什么？说明市场还没有形成真正可靠的上涨基础，资金的信心和方向都存在严重问题。
         更让我担心的是，市场反弹依然离不开科技故事会。半导体、算力硬件等高估值方向轮番表现，AI漫剧、光伏、机器人等题材又不断制造短线热点。周三半导体领涨，周五算力硬件却成为重灾区，剑桥科技、澳弘电子跌停，工业富联、生益科技大幅下跌。这样的市场结构，哪里像一轮健康的牛市？热点每天换主角，资金追逐的仍然是短期题材，而不是企业真正的盈利能力。
         我并不否定科技产业的发展，也不反对有真实业绩支撑的科技企业上涨，但把没有业绩支撑的概念炒上天，绝不是推动A股持续上涨的正确道路。此前的调整已经给市场敲响了警钟，如果现在又把科技故事会当成救市主力，那么下一次泡沫破裂，市场还要承受多大的代价？这才是我最不希望看到的事情。

Welcome to the Weekly KAOS — UrbanKaoboy’s end-of-week roundup covering Macro and Geopolitics, where I try and tease out the most impactful bits of the week.

Themes of the Week
There is an iconic scene in the original Star Wars (Episode IV: A New Hope) when the Millennium Falcon jumps to hyperspace expecting a clean run to Alderaan, only to find itself jolted back into realspace early, straight into the debris field resulting from the Death Star’s destruction of the planet.

That is a good Mental Model for how I perceive the AI Buildout/US Economy, given this week’s decisive Democratic sweep of the midterms. The AI Buildout (Han Solo) has been piloting the US Economy (Millennium Falcon), and last night’s Blue Tsunami was the “great disturbance in the Force” that Republicans and the AI trade felt in the same instant. The biggest upset was Texas turning blue for the first time in roughly three decades, and the governor-elect campaigned on a moratorium on new data centers. A buildout that runs on permits, grid interconnection, water, and tax abatements does not love a forced deceleration.

What makes it worse is that the front of the Bullwhip I described last week was already cracking before a single vote was counted. Anthropic’s revised S-1 showed revenue growth decelerating hard, and in my read it is Open Source models forcing accelerated token price discounts at the demand end. Stack three forces together (the Debt Governor, a slowdown at the front of the Bullwhip potentially leading to amplified slowdowns upstream at the end of the Bullwhip, and now a politically forced premature deceleration at the same upstream end of the Bullwhip) and you start to have the ingredients for a serious challenge to the AI trade and the overall economy.

I hold all of this as concern and open question rather than prediction. There may even be a silver lining, because letting the air out of the balloon slowly beats popping it, and a forced deceleration could finally mollify the Debt Governor that has been choking the whole complex. Wednesday’s blistering but differentiated rally gave some hints of this, but alas, Thursday’s rout reversed everything and then some.
